
## From one species to a community

A conservation plan needs an answer for every species, not one. We could fit 108 separate models, but a joint model does better: it fits all species together, shares information between them through hidden site effects that act on many species at once, and estimates how species go together after the environment is accounted for.

Fitting this model for 108 mammals takes several minutes on a fast laptop, so we use a fit prepared earlier (5,000 burn-in and 5,000 kept iterations, two chains). The summaries below come from it. If you want to run the occJSDM output functions on the full fit, your instructor can share the file.

```{r load}
fit <- read_fit_summary()      # a list of tables: occ, params, diagnostics and assoc
status <- species_status()
sites <- site_covariates()
m <- load_mammal()
presence <- (rowsum(m$OTU, m$info$Site) > 0) * 1   # as in Session 1: 1 if any PCR at the site was positive
sites_detected <- colSums(presence)
```

The full fitted model is too large for a 4 GB session, so `read_fit_summary()` loads tables taken from it. On a fit of your own you would make those tables with the occJSDM functions you used on the dhole in Session 2. The chunk below shows how, and is not run in class.

```{r from-a-fit, eval = FALSE}
library(occJSDM)
fit_full <- readRDS("fit_Mammal_d4_fixed.rds")     # the full mammal fit, 236 MB

# Probability of presence given the detections (cond_mean), and before them (psi_mean):
# one row per site, one column per species
cond <- computeConditionalOccupancyProbs(fit_full)
psi <- computePredictiveOccupancyProbs(fit_full)
occ <- tibble(Site = rep(rownames(cond), ncol(cond)), otu_id = rep(colnames(cond), each = nrow(cond)),
              cond_mean = as.vector(cond), psi_mean = as.vector(psi))

# Detection rates: posterior draws in fit_full$results_output$p_output and q_output, as in Session 2

# Convergence: the largest R-hat per species, for detection and for the occupancy effects
diag <- returnConvergenceDiagnostics(fit_full)
species_ids <- colnames(cond)
diagnostics <- diag |>
  mutate(otu_id = if_else(label2 %in% species_ids, label2, label1),     # the species name is in one of the two
         group = if_else(param %in% c("beta0_psi", "beta_psi"), "rhat_effects", "rhat_detection")) |>
  group_by(otu_id, group) |>
  summarise(rhat = max(rhat, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = rhat)

# Associations: lower, median and upper residual correlation for each pair of species
sig <- returnResidualCorrelationMatrix(fit_full)   # 3 x species x species
pairs <- which(upper.tri(sig[1, , ]), arr.ind = TRUE)
assoc <- tibble(otu_a = species_ids[pairs[, 1]], otu_b = species_ids[pairs[, 2]],
                lo = sig[1, , ][pairs], median = sig[2, , ][pairs], hi = sig[3, , ][pairs])
```

## Can we trust the computation?

With 108 species there are hundreds of parameters. For each species we take the largest R-hat in two groups: its detection parameters (the true- and false-positive rates and the effects of the collection covariates), and its covariate effects on occupancy. As in Session 2, R-hat near 1 means the chains agree. Here we call a group settled if its largest R-hat is at most 1.1.

```{r convergence}
conv <- fit$diagnostics |>
  mutate(sites_detected = sites_detected[otu_id],
         detection_settled = rhat_detection <= 1.1,
         effects_settled = rhat_effects <= 1.1)
conv |> count(detection_settled, effects_settled)
conv |>
  filter(!detection_settled | !effects_settled) |>
  arrange(sites_detected) |>
  select(species, sites_detected, rhat_detection, rhat_effects)
```

```{r rhat-plot}
conv |>
  pivot_longer(c(rhat_detection, rhat_effects), names_to = "parameters", values_to = "rhat") |>
  ggplot(aes(rhat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.1, linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ parameters, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Largest R-hat per species", y = "Number of species",
       title = "Detection has settled for almost every species; the covariate effects have not") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Detection has settled for all but four species. The covariate effects are worse: for 29 species at least one effect has not settled, and 30 species fail one check or the other. Half of those 30 were detected at six sites or fewer, where there is little information, but the list also includes common species such as *Rattus tanezumi*, detected at 84 sites. The dhole passes both checks.

The cure is a longer run, which takes too long for class. Until then, do not read the covariate effects of these 30 species, and treat their probabilities of presence with care, because those probabilities are built from the same effects. This is a limit of this fit, not a reason to drop the whole analysis.

## How reliable is each species' detection?

The model gives each species its own true-positive and false-positive rates.

```{r detection-profile}
profile <- fit$params |> left_join(status[, c("otu_id", "local_status", "order")], by = "otu_id")
ggplot(profile, aes(q_mean, p_mean, colour = local_status)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = q_lo, xmax = q_hi), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = p_lo, ymax = p_hi), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(wild = "grey30", dom = "firebrick", wild_or_dom = "darkorange"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "False-positive rate per PCR", y = "True-positive rate per PCR",
       title = "Detection quality varies a lot between species") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r worst-fp}
profile |>
  arrange(desc(q_mean)) |>
  transmute(species, local_status, false_positive = round(q_mean, 3), true_positive = round(p_mean, 2)) |>
  head(10)
```

The highest false-positive rates belong to species detected at most sites. They include the pig and cattle, whose DNA probably reaches rivers from farms and settlements, but also several common small mammals. The model cannot say why a species has a high rate, only that its raw detections overstate where it lives.

## Probability of presence at every site

For each site and each species, the model gives the probability that the species is present given what was detected. These are the numbers the conservation plan will use.

```{r occupancy}
occ <- fit$occ |>
  left_join(status |> select(otu_id, order, family, iucn, china_red_list, local_status), by = "otu_id")
occ |> select(Site, species, cond_mean, psi_mean) |> head()
```

`cond_mean` is the probability of presence given the detections: the one for asking "is species X at site 12?". `psi_mean` is the probability of presence before this species' own detections at the site are weighed. It comes from the site's covariates plus the hidden site effects, and those hidden effects were estimated from what all the species detected at the site have in common. So `psi_mean` is not a prediction for a site nobody surveyed. That would need the covariates alone, which this workshop does not cover. Both are posterior means. The package does not yet return intervals for these, which we come back to in Session 4.

```{r certainty}
ggplot(occ, aes(cond_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "grey40") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Probability of presence given the detections", y = "Site-species pairs (log scale)",
       title = "Most site-species pairs are settled; a minority are uncertain") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## How many species are at each site?

The raw count of species detected at a site and the model's expected number of species are different things. The expected number is the sum of the probabilities of presence.

```{r richness}
richness <- occ |>
  group_by(Site) |>
  summarise(expected = sum(cond_mean), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(detected = rowSums(presence)[Site]) |>
  left_join(sites, by = "Site")

richness |>
  summarise(detected = mean(detected), expected = mean(expected))
```

```{r richness-map, fig.width = 10}
richness |>
  pivot_longer(c(detected, expected), names_to = "measure", values_to = "species") |>
  ggplot(aes(Xs.1, Xs.2, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "Species") +
  coord_quickmap() + labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Richness can be split by taxonomic order, to see which groups drive the pattern.

```{r richness-order}
occ |>
  group_by(order, Site) |>
  summarise(expected = sum(cond_mean), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(order) |>
  summarise(mean_per_site = round(mean(expected), 2), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(mean_per_site))
```

The saved table `data-derived/occupancy_long.csv` has one row per site and species, with taxonomy and conservation status attached. Session 4 reads it.

## Which species go together?

After the environment is accounted for, some species still occur together more than chance would suggest. The model estimates these residual associations as correlations. We keep only pairs whose 95% interval excludes zero.

```{r associations}
assoc <- fit$assoc |>
  filter(lo > 0 | hi < 0) |>
  left_join(status[, c("otu_id", "species")], by = c("otu_a" = "otu_id")) |> rename(species_a = species) |>
  left_join(status[, c("otu_id", "species")], by = c("otu_b" = "otu_id")) |> rename(species_b = species)
c(credible_pairs = nrow(assoc), positive = sum(assoc$median > 0), negative = sum(assoc$median < 0))
assoc |> arrange(desc(median)) |> transmute(species_a, species_b, correlation = round(median, 2)) |> head(10)
```

Every association that survives is positive: no pair is credibly less likely to co-occur than chance. The strongest are between close relatives (the *Rattus* species), between livestock (cattle and buffalo), and between the dhole and *Canis lupus*, a name that also covers domestic dogs. An association is not an interaction. Two species can co-occur because they share an unmeasured habitat, because DNA from both is washed into the same water, or because they really do interact. The table is a place to start asking, not an answer.

```{r mcp, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !mcp_off}
cat('**Ask the assistant.** Posit Assistant can help you write R against the tables above. Try these, and read the code it writes before you run it.

- Which species have a false-positive rate above 0.1, and what share of them are domestic?
- Map the expected richness of carnivores only.
- Which five species are most likely to be present at the site with the highest expected richness?

The assistant is a helper for R here. The occJSDM tools it used on Wednesday need data and a new fit, which we do not do today.
')
```

## What you take away

- A joint model gives a probability of presence for every species at every site, with the false positives accounted for.
- Check convergence for every species, and know which ones are flagged.
- Expected richness and raw richness tell different stories.
- Session 4 uses `occupancy_long.csv` to ask where to protect.
